title: Like the ocean
hookLine: nibbana compared to the ocean, to a mountain peak, to space (Milinda, Book 4)

lines: NO. BUT ITS QUALITIES, BY SIMILE.
cards: Try describing the color blue to someone who has never seen color. Sooner or later the words turn into likenesses: cool like water, open like the sky. The king hits the same wall.

He asks Nagasena about nibbana, the end of craving and suffering that the whole path points toward. Can you show me its shape, its size, its color, how long it lasts? No, says Nagasena; it can't be shown that way.
Then is there nothing to say at all? There is, Nagasena answers. Its qualities can be pointed to, one simile at a time.

teach.b: First, like the ocean. The ocean, Nagasena says, is vast and boundless, and all the rivers flowing into it never fill it up. Nibbana too is not filled by all the beings who reach it.
The ocean keeps no corpse; it washes it ashore. Nibbana keeps none of the corpses of the defilements: greed, hatred and delusion. Second, like a mountain peak.
A peak is lofty and cannot be shaken. It's hard to climb, and seeds don't take root on the bare summit.

teach.h: PEAK: HIGH, UNSHAKABLE, HARD TO CLIMB.
teach.b: Nibbana is high, unshakable, hard to reach, a place where the defilements can't grow, and free from liking and disliking, as a peak favors no one.
Third, like space. Space is not born and does not grow old. It does not die or pass away.
It can't be conquered, and thieves can't carry it off. It rests on nothing, it has no end, and birds move through it freely. Nibbana, Nagasena says, has those qualities.
Fourth, why similes. Nagasena isn't hiding something; he's being honest about what words can do.

teach.h: A SET OF WINDOWS, NOT A SHAPE.
teach.b: A shape would make nibbana one more thing in the world, something with edges, something to grab.
A simile gives a direction instead: look toward the open sea, the high summit, the clear sky, and keep looking past them. The king asked for a description and got a set of windows.
Each one shows a little; none is the view itself. It's Nagasena's way of saying: this is real, and it's not an object.

how: Buddhist teachers often speak of nibbana by simile rather than definition, and Nagasena's comparisons to the ocean, a mountain peak and space are among those retold.

o: a heaven where the good go to live after death
a blank nothing, where all things simply stop
the path's goal, shown only by likeness: sea, peak, sky

games.q: like the ocean: tap the pairs.
p: no seeds take root on it
nibbana can't be shown that way

s: Nagasena refuses to say anything at all about nibbana
he says it can't be shown by shape or size, but its qualities can be pointed to by simile.
in the simile, space can't be carried off by thieves
it is not born, does not die, rests on nothing, and can't be stolen or conquered.
the ocean simile says nibbana gets fuller as more beings reach it
the ocean is never filled by the rivers, and nibbana is not filled by all who reach it.

games.q: you're Nagasena. the king asks you to show him nibbana's shape, size and color. what do you do?
o: describe it as a heavenly place.
say nothing can be said about it.
say it has no shape, but point to its qualities by simile.
games.why: he says it can't be shown by shape, then compares its qualities to the ocean, a mountain peak, and space.

practice: Go to a window, step outside, or remember the sky from this morning, and let your eyes rest on the open part, not the clouds or buildings. Notice that it holds everything that moves through it and keeps none of it.
Then let that openness be the background for the breath, with thoughts moving through like birds.

wordCard.voice: Nibbana. What Nagasena points to only by simile, the ocean, the mountain peak and space, since it can't be shown by shape.

orig.note: Pali: space, sky. one of Nagasena's similes for nibbana.

carryVoice: Your line: like space. Unborn, resting on nothing, keeping nothing. That's day eight hundred seventy-three.

sources.ref: Milindapanha, Book 4 (the similes for nibbana: the ocean, space, the mountain peak)
